title: Relative smooth centralizers and normalizers of split tori
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], and let $G\to S$ be a smooth affine group scheme of finite presentation [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Group schemes over $S$ have the multiplication, inverse and identity diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme], with base $S$. Write $\mathbf G_{m,S}=\operatorname{Spec}_S\mathcal O_S[t,t^{-1}]$ with multiplication of units, and let $T=\mathbf G_{m,S}^r$ for $r\geq0$. Suppose $j:T\hookrightarrow G$ is a closed subgroup immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. For every $S$-scheme $W$, let $C(W)$ consist of $g\in G(W)$ commuting with all $t\in T(W')$ after every $W$-scheme extension $W'\to W$, and let $N(W)$ consist of $g\in G(W)$ such that conjugation by $g$ preserves $T_W$ as a subgroup functor. Then $C$ and $N$ are represented by smooth affine $S$-group schemes of finite presentation, closed in $G$, and their formation commutes with arbitrary base change. The tangent module at the identity $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is a finite locally free $\mathcal O_S$-module (Zariski locally a free module of finite rank), and $\operatorname{Lie}(C)=\mathfrak g^T$ inside $\mathfrak g$, compatibly with arbitrary base change; invariance means the full torus coaction, not its differential. For every $\sigma\in\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbf Z)$, the subfunctor $N_\sigma$ whose conjugation action on $T_W$ is the Laurent-monomial automorphism $\sigma$ is an open and closed subscheme of $N$. The $N_\sigma$ cover $N$ and commute with base change. For $r=0$ the matrix group has one element.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/luminysga3smf.pdf . Proposition 2.1.2, printed pp.56-60 (normalizer); Lemma 2.2.4, printed pp.64-66 (centralizer and Lie invariants); Corollary B.2.7 and the Laurent-character description of split-torus automorphisms (open-and-closed action-matrix loci). These are structural inputs to Proposition 3.1.9, not an openness conclusion.

proof.text: Work over an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq S$, and write $G=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $T=\operatorname{Spec}A[M]$, $M=\mathbf Z^r$, with $A[M]=A[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Write $q:B\twoheadrightarrow A[M]$ for $j$. Choose finitely many algebra generators $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ of $B$. The composite surjection $A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow B\twoheadrightarrow A[M]$ has finitely generated kernel by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-presentation-surjection-kernel-fg], since $A[M]=A[t_i,z_i]/(t_i z_i-1)_i$ is finitely presented. Its image in $B$ is $I=\ker q$, so choose generators $f_1,\ldots,f_d$ of $I$. This works without a noetherian assumption.

source.place: Proposition 2.1.2 and Remark 2.2.7: explicit Laurent-coefficient version of the closed-condition argument; finite relations justified by Stacks Tag 00R2, algebra.tex lemma-finite-presentation-independent

proof.text: Let $c:G\times_S T\to G$ be $(g,t)\mapsto gj(t)g^{-1}$. For each $b_i$, expand $c^*(b_i)-1\otimes q(b_i)\in B\otimes_A A[M]=B[M]$ in the Laurent basis. Let $K_C\subset B$ be the ideal generated by all its coefficients. There are finitely many coefficients. For every $A$-algebra $R$ and $g:B\to R$, their images vanish exactly when the two maps $T_R\rightrightarrows G_R$, $t\mapsto gj(t)g^{-1}$ and $t\mapsto j(t)$, agree: equality on the algebra generators suffices, and Laurent monomials remain an $R$-basis. This is precisely the universal commuting condition, including all further test extensions. Hence $\operatorname{Spec}(B/K_C)$ represents $C$ on this affine base and is closed affine and finitely presented over it.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.4 and Remark 2.2.7: equality of the two maps expressed by their coordinate coefficients

proof.text: For the normalizer use both maps $c_\pm(g,t)=g^{\pm1}j(t)g^{\mp1}$. Let $K_N\subset B$ be generated by the Laurent coefficients of $c_+^*(f_a)$ and $c_-^*(f_a)$ for $1\leq a\leq d$. Vanishing means both conjugation maps $T_R\to G_R$ factor through $T_R$: the first gives $gT_Rg^{-1}\subseteq T_R$, the second gives the reverse inclusion after conjugating. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}(B/K_N)$ represents exactly $N$, and is closed affine and finitely presented. The same coefficients after $A\to A'$ define the base-changed functors: $A'[M]$ still has the Laurent basis, and $\ker(B\otimes_A A'\to A'[M])$ is the image of $I\otimes_A A'$. The latter assertion follows by tensoring $B/I=A[M]$ and right exactness, or directly by the quotient presentation. The local ideals on overlapping affine base opens therefore agree, since they impose the same universal equations, and glue. Multiplication, identity and inverse preserve commuting, respectively normalizing, on all test schemes, so their restrictions give group schemes. This proves all representation, finite-presentation, closedness and arbitrary-base-change assertions globally.

source.place: Proposition 2.1.2 and Remark 2.2.7: coefficient factorization conditions; both conjugation directions are imposed explicitly

proof.text: Prove formal smoothness of $C$. Let $R\to R/J$ be a square-zero quotient over $S$, and $g_0\in C(R/J)$. The base change $G_R$ is smooth: its finite presentation follows by tensoring a finite presentation, and each affine square-zero lifting diagram over $R$ is the identical diagram over $S$, so formal smoothness follows from that of $G$. Smoothness of $G$ in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] supplies $g\in G(R)$ lifting $g_0$. The homomorphisms $f_1=\operatorname{Int}(g)\circ j_R$ and $f_2=j_R$ from $T_R$ to $G_R$ have equal reductions. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-infinitesimal-conjugacy] to obtain $u\equiv1\pmod J$ with $\operatorname{Int}(u)\circ f_1=f_2$. Then $ug$ lifts $g_0$ and centralizes $T_R$ as a subgroup functor. Every square-zero lifting test is solved, so $C\to S$ is formally smooth. Its already proved finite presentation gives smoothness by the same definition.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.4, printed pp.65-66, infinitesimal conjugation argument; Corollary B.2.6 with equality of homomorphisms, which directly gives centralization

proof.text: Now let $g_0\in N(R/J)$. Its conjugation automorphism $\alpha_0$ of $T_{R/J}$ is a locally constant $\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbf Z)$-valued function by [lem-sfb-relative-split-torus-matrix-sheaf]. The spectra of $R$ and $R/J$ have the same topology because every prime contains the square-zero ideal. Thus this function uniquely specifies an automorphism $\alpha$ of $T_R$, reducing to $\alpha_0$, by that same node. Lift $g_0$ to $g\in G(R)$ by smoothness. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-infinitesimal-conjugacy] to $\operatorname{Int}(g)\circ j_R$ and $j_R\circ\alpha$, which agree modulo $J$. The resulting $ug$ lifts $g_0$ and induces $\alpha$ on $T_R$, so belongs to $N(R)$. Consequently $N$ is formally smooth and, being finitely presented, smooth. The argument permits disconnected $\operatorname{Spec}R$ and does not assume a single constant matrix on it.

source.place: Proposition 2.1.2 smoothness proof, printed pp.57-58; Corollary B.2.6; split-torus character classification in Appendix B.1

proof.text: Let $e:S\to G$ be the identity. By [lem-ag-smooth-relative-differentials-finite-locally-free], $\Omega^1_{G/S}$ is finite locally free. Pulling a local basis back along $e$ and taking its dual proves that $\mathfrak g=(e^*\Omega^1_{G/S})^\vee$ is finite locally free. Its sections on an affine test base $\operatorname{Spec}R$ are the kernel of $G(R[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)\to G(R)$: a lift of the identity augmentation has the form $b\mapsto e^*(b)+\epsilon D(b)$, and multiplicativity says exactly that $D$ is an $A$-derivation into $R$. The universal property in [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] identifies these with the dual cotangent module. This description is linear and natural. The differential base-change isomorphism [lem-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials-base-change] followed by $e^*$ identifies identity cotangent modules after every base change; dualization commutes with base change because it does so on each finite free local basis. Thus $\mathfrak g$ commutes with arbitrary base change, as does $\operatorname{Lie}(C)$ by the same argument applied to smooth $C$.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.4, printed p.66, identity tangent bundles; Stacks Tags 02G1 and 00RV for differentials and their base change

proof.text: Conjugation by $T$ induces its adjoint coaction on $\mathfrak g$ by applying the identity-tangent construction to $c$. Locally on $S$ where $\mathfrak g$ is finite free, [lem-sfb-relative-torus-bundle-weights] identifies its invariant submodule with the weight-zero summand, finite projective and compatible with every scalar extension. In the dual-number description of the previous step, a tangent vector $v$ factors through $C$ exactly when $\operatorname{Int}(j(t))(1+\epsilon v)=1+\epsilon v$ as maps on every test extension. The left side is $1+\epsilon\operatorname{Ad}(t)v$ by the definition of the differential of conjugation. Hence this condition is exactly $\operatorname{Ad}(t)v=v$ universally, equivalently coaction $v\mapsto v\otimes1$. This proves $\operatorname{Lie}(C)=\mathfrak g^T$ as submodules, not merely on geometric fibres. Both descriptions and the zero-weight summand commute with every base change. In particular this uses invariance under the whole torus and never replaces it by invariance under its differential.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.4, printed p.66, invariant tangent subbundle; dual-number computation of the fixed tangent functor

proof.text: Over the scheme $N$, the universal normalizer point induces an actual group-scheme automorphism of $T_N$. By [lem-sfb-relative-split-torus-matrix-sheaf] it gives a locally constant function $a:|N|\to\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbf Z)$. For each $\sigma$, its inverse image is open and closed; equip it with the corresponding open subscheme structure. A morphism $W\to N$ factors through this subscheme exactly when the conjugation automorphism on $T_W$ is $\sigma$, by the base-change naturality in that node. It therefore represents $N_\sigma$. The inverse images cover $N$ and pull back to the same inverse images after arbitrary base change. This is an open cover of schemes; on a disconnected test scheme a point can have different matrices on different open-and-closed parts. For $r=0$, $T=S$ is trivial, both coefficient ideals are zero, $C=N=G$, $\mathfrak g^T=\mathfrak g$, and there is just the unique empty matrix, so all assertions include rank zero.
